bible_refs.note: κυριεύει τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἐφ’ ὅσον χρόνον ζῇ, repeated twice; cited inline at the first.
ἐθανατώθητε τῷ νόμῳ διὰ τοῦ σώματος τοῦ Χριστοῦ.
Lemma, then paraphrased with εἰς τὸ καρποφορῆσαι τῷ θανάτῳ.

choices.why: ἐπιδημία: Christ’s coming (the Incarnation); rendered “his coming”.

choices.term: κἂν εἰ ἕλοιτο τοῦτο δρᾶν ἐννόμως

choices.why: κἂν εἰ ἕλοιτο τοῦτο δρᾶν ἐννόμως: the adverb ἐννόμως qualifies the remarriage; rendered “even if she chooses to do this, since she does it lawfully”.

choices.term: εἰ μηκέτι χρηματίζουσιν ὡς ζῶντες ἐν κόσμῳ

choices.why: εἰ μηκέτι χρηματίζουσιν ὡς ζῶντες ἐν κόσμῳ kept as a condition (“if they are no longer reckoned…”), and the optative ποιοῖντο ἄν as “may lead”.
οὐκ ἔξω γεγονόσι: the object (the flesh, i.e. bodily life) is implied; Cyril’s point is that Paul’s hearers were still in the body, so “flesh” in Romans 7:5 must mean the fleshly mind.

τοῦτο παρείς: rendered literally “leaving this aside”; the referent is probably the law (in Galatians 5:17 Paul sets flesh against Spirit without naming the law between them), but the English keeps the Greek's open pronoun rather than supplying it.

choices.why: καίτοι πῶς οὐκ ἀληθὲς … οὐκ ἔξω γεγονόσι: kept as a rhetorical question (“who would deny…?”); the implied thing not left is the bodily flesh, so the reading text says “the body” to keep Cyril's contrast with the fleshly mind clear.

pass_a_gloss: …every law (νόμος) and of those under law; for to all under sceptres of kings laws define the to-be-done and the not; they are strong among the still living; if one of those under law be released from the embodied life, he stripped off together with life also the authority (ἐξουσία) of the laws; for if he has ceased to offend (πλημμελεῖν), the law too will be idle upon him. True then that it lords (κυριεύει) over the man as long as he lives. And what is the aim (σκοπός) of the saying, necessary to say: two useful things he brings in by it: we, he says, the co-buried with Christ through baptism (βάπτισμα), the dead to sin, have come outside the authority of the law, for we have been re-elemented (μετεστοιχειώμεθα) into another life; but those before the sojourn (ἐπιδημία), not yet having undergone the death understood in Christ, were living still to sin. The law ruled them as living, just as the husband the wife; for as the woman under a husband, the one lawfully cohabiting still alive, does not make un-liable the union under another; but if he die, he says, she will lie outside penalty (δίκη), even if she choose to do this lawfully; in equal manner I think those not yet having the deadening (νέκρωσις) of sin in Christ, living as in it, fittingly fared under law too; for it lords over the man as long as he lives; but those already become under grace (χάρις) in Christ, through which they died to sin and were deadened to the flesh, that is to the passions (πάθη) of the flesh, if they are no longer styled as living in the world, would make blameless the life outside law; for they were put to death, as I said, through the body of Christ, and died to the law being justified (δικαιούμενοι) through faith. [Lemma Romans 7:5] Flesh he names the fleshly mind (φρόνημα), as elsewhere [Romans 8:8]; and how not true that to those initiated (μυσταγωγουμένοις) by him as not having come outside he enjoins such things? What he wishes to show, necessary to inquire: when we lived as citizens fleshly, the earthy mind ruling in us, then worked in us the passions of the flesh through the law to bear fruit to death. What then? one might say: the passions of the flesh were brought in through the law? Then how shall we free it of charges? Not through law were moved in us the passions of the flesh, but born rather from inborn pleasure (ἡδονή), and plunders the weak mind; this he makes manifest saying [Galatians 5:17]. Now passing this by, he says the flesh marches out against the spirit, putting nothing between. Therefore not through the law the passions of the flesh move in us, rather naturally (φυσικῶς); and the paradox, they stand up against the wills (θελήματα) of the law, as he himself somewhere…
pass_b_english: …every law and for those who are under law.
For laws define, for all who live under the sceptres of kings, what must be done and what must not; but they have force only among those who are still alive.

If someone who is under law departs from life in the body, he has put off, together with his life, the authority of the laws as well. For if he has ceased from wrongdoing, the law too will surely have nothing more to do with him.
It is true, then, that the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives (Romans 7:1).
We must also say what the aim of the passage is. He brings two useful points into it.
We, he says, who have been buried with Christ through baptism (Romans 6:4), who have died to sin (Romans 6:2), have passed outside the authority of the law, for we have been remade for another life.
But those who lived before his coming, not yet having undergone the death that is understood in Christ, were still living to sin.
So the law ruled over them as over the living, just as a husband rules over his wife.

For as a married woman, while the man lawfully joined to her is still alive, cannot unite with another man without answering for it, yet if he dies, he says, she will be free of penalty even if she chooses to do this, since she does it lawfully (Romans 7:2–3), in the same way, I think, those who did not yet have the deadening of sin in Christ, but were living, as it were, in sin, were rightly under law as well; for the law has dominion over a person for as long as he lives.

But those who have already come under the grace that is in Christ, through which they have died to sin and been put to death to the flesh, that is, to the passions of the flesh, may lead a life outside the law without blame, if they are no longer reckoned as people living in the world (Colossians 2:20).
For, as I said, they have been put to death through the body of Christ, and they died to the law (Romans 7:4), being justified through faith.
“For while we were in the flesh, the passions of sins, which were through the law, were at work,” and so on (Romans 7:5).
By “flesh” he means the fleshly mind, as he says elsewhere too: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Romans 8:8).
And yet who would deny that he gives such instructions to those he was initiating into the mystery as to people who had not left the body?
What he means to show must be examined closely.
When we lived in a fleshly way, he says, and the earthly mind ruled in us, then the passions of the flesh were at work in us through the law, to bear fruit for death (Romans 7:5).
“What then?” someone might say. “Were the passions of the flesh brought in through the law? Then how shall we clear the law of the charges against it?”
What do we say to this? The passions of the flesh were not stirred in us through the law. Rather, they are born from inborn pleasure and they plunder the weak mind.
He makes this plain to us when he says, “The flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other” (Galatians 5:17).
Here, leaving this aside, he says that the flesh is set in battle against the Spirit, with nothing placed between them.
So the passions of the flesh are not stirred in us through the law, but rather by nature; and, strange to say, they rise up against the will of the law, as he himself somewhere…

review_notes: Staged row fixed in place in tr1.json. Every clause checked against the source. (1) The ὥσπερ … κατὰ τὸν ἴσον τρόπον sentence was split across two paragraphs (one ended on a comma, the next began lower-case); merged into one paragraph. (2) καίτοι πῶς οὐκ ἀληθὲς ὡς οὐκ ἔξω γεγονόσι …: 'And surely it is true' lost both καίτοι ('and yet') and the rhetorical question, and 'had not left the flesh' clashed with the claim just made that 'flesh' here means the fleshly mind; now 'And yet who would deny that he gives such instructions … as to people who had not left the body?' (3) τοῦτο παρείς: the English supplied 'the law' as the object; the Greek has only 'this', so now 'leaving this aside'. Translator notes updated for (2) and (3). Negation (οὐ διὰ νόμου … κεκίνηται πάθη), the objector's voice (φαίη τίς ἄν) and the optative ποιοῖντο ἄν ('may lead') checked; refs Romans 7:1, 6:4, 6:2, 7:2–3, Colossians 2:20, Romans 7:4, 7:5, 8:8, Galatians 5:17 correct.
Copy-text: PG 74; Fragmenta in Romanos via Khazarzar (Fragmenta in sancti Pauli epistulam ad Romanos.pdf).

The row opens mid-sentence (παντὸς καὶ τῶν ὑπὸ νόμον completes ὅρος οὗτος γενικὸς κατά τε νόμου from u03-rem-mid) and ends mid-sentence at ὡς αὐτός που; the sentence continues in u04-open (φησὶν ὁ Παῦλος).
ἐπιδημία: Christ’s coming (the Incarnation); rendered “his coming”.
κἂν εἰ ἕλοιτο τοῦτο δρᾶν ἐννόμως: the adverb ἐννόμως qualifies the remarriage; rendered “even if she chooses to do this, since she does it lawfully”.
εἰ μηκέτι χρηματίζουσιν ὡς ζῶντες ἐν κόσμῳ kept as a condition (“if they are no longer reckoned…”), and the optative ποιοῖντο ἄν as “may lead”.
οὐκ ἔξω γεγονόσι: the object (the flesh, i.e. bodily life) is implied; Cyril’s point is that Paul’s hearers were still in the body, so “flesh” in Romans 7:5 must mean the fleshly mind.

τοῦτο παρείς: rendered literally “leaving this aside”; the referent is probably the law (in Galatians 5:17 Paul sets flesh against Spirit without naming the law between them), but the English keeps the Greek's open pronoun rather than supplying it.

καίτοι πῶς οὐκ ἀληθὲς … οὐκ ἔξω γεγονόσι: kept as a rhetorical question (“who would deny…?”); the implied thing not left is the bodily flesh, so the reading text says “the body” to keep Cyril's contrast with the fleshly mind clear.
πνεῦμα in Galatians 5:17 and the following sentence capitalised as the Holy Spirit, following the common reading of the verse.
